answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From a letter Marie wrote to her brother, dated March 18, 1894. It is printed in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie: A Biography (1937), translated by Vincent Sheean, p. 116. The English wording is Sheean’s translation and is confirmed in a full-text scan of the 1937 printing.

source.excerpt: I want you to pass your doctor’s thesis. … It seems that life is not easy for any of us. But what of that? We must have perseverance and above all confidence in ourselves. We must believe that we are gifted for something, and that this thing, at whatever cost, must be attained. Perhaps everything will turn out very well, at the moment when we least expect it.
trail: 1894: Marie, then a student in Paris, writes to her brother. The letter is dated March 18, 1894, in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie, p. 116 ↗.

1937: Eve Curie’s biography of her mother appears in English, translated by Vincent Sheean. It prints the letter, then on p. 158 quotes the line again in the short form now in circulation (1937 Literary Guild printing ↗).
Today: Wikiquote’s Marie Curie page ↗ lists the full English wording in its main Quotes section, with a French text and a citation to Eve Curie’s biography, Part 2, p. 116.
source.excerptNote: In the letter as printed on p. 116, the sentence begins “It seems that life is not easy…” Eve Curie quotes it again on p. 158 (ch. XII, “The Discovery of Radium”), introducing it with “It was barely four years before that Marie had written:” That second quotation starts at “Life is not easy for any of us,” which is the form that circulates today.

author.bio: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Marie Curie moved to Paris to study and became a pioneer of research on radioactivity. With Pierre Curie she discovered polonium and radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences, physics and chemistry.

misattribution.heading: Small wording drift, not a fake
misattribution.intro: This is one of the few popular Marie Curie lines with a solid source. The versions online differ only slightly from the printed text.

items.who: “Life is not easy for any of us”
items.why: In the letter as printed on p. 116, the sentence begins “It seems that life is not easy for any of us.” The trimmed opening comes from the biography itself: Eve Curie quotes the passage again on p. 158 without “It seems that” (full text ↗).

Some sites have “gifted in something” instead of “gifted for something.” Wikiquote lists that variant in a second entry, cited only to the Today in Science History website. The 1937 translation reads “gifted for something” in both places (Wikiquote ↗).

Most quote sites print the line with no recipient or date. In the source it is part of a private letter to her brother, dated March 18, 1894, encouraging him to finish his doctor’s thesis (1937 biography ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The popular wording is genuine Marie Curie in Vincent Sheean’s 1937 English translation. It comes from her letter to her brother dated March 18, 1894, as printed in Eve Curie’s Madame Curie, p. 116 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Marie wrote the letter as a student in Paris, poor and working alone. On the same page, the biography describes how she stretched a small scholarship to stay longer at the university. The advice is for her brother, whom she urges to pass his doctor’s thesis, but it also describes how she was living herself.

Her daughter Eve came back to the line in the chapter on the discovery of radium. There she presents it as the resolve behind that work: “That ‘something’ was to throw science upon a path hitherto unsuspected.”
